documents.abstract: This article examines virtual production as a critical infrastructure of contemporary audiovisual practice, moving beyond its restricted understanding as a technical innovation or a set of tools designed to optimize shooting processes. The objective of the study is to analyze, through an integrative literature review, how specialized scholarship conceptualizes virtual production in relation to three strategic dimensions: the reconfiguration of the audiovisual pipeline, structural inequalities of access, and the conditions of sustainability and governance within the production ecosystem. Methodologically, a qualitative thematic review was conducted. From an initial pool of 68 records, selection criteria based on thematic relevance, conceptual density, and interpretative contribution were applied, resulting in a final corpus of 29 unique texts published between 2016 and 2026, including peer-reviewed articles, industry reports, doctoral theses, and technical documents. The analysis was structured around four interconnected axes: (1) virtual production as a sociotechnical system and critical infrastructure; (2) the transition from a linear production model toward iterative convergence and early integration across pre-production, production, and post-production; (3) unequal access, labor transformations, and professional training under the notion of “conditional democratization”; and (4) ecosystemic sustainability linked to technological governance, impact assessment, technical memory, and local capacity building. The findings indicate that virtual production not only transforms visual representation or the physical set but also reorganizes the material, informational, and institutional foundations of audiovisual labor. Furthermore, its expansion does not guarantee automatic democratization, as it depends on pre-existing infrastructures, specialized human capital, and stable collaborative frameworks. The study offers a critical and integrative reading of virtual production as a structural phenomenon shaping twenty-first-century audiovisual practice, particularly relevant to Latin America and Central America.

Hospitality research has often viewed motivation as the primary mechanism linking managerial practices to employee behavior. However, less attention has been paid to how employees interpret such practices before motivational responses emerge. Drawing on professional identity research, this study examines Professional Identity as an interpretive mechanism linking employees’ perceptions of Rewards and Transformational Leadership to Motivation and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Using survey data from 325 frontline hotel employees in South Korea, we test an individual-level model connecting Developmental Rewards, Material Rewards, Transformational Leadership, Professional Identity, Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, and OCB. The results show significant indirect associations between Developmental Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation and between Transformational Leadership and Intrinsic Motivation through Professional Identity. Developmental Rewards and Transformational Leadership were also indirectly associated with OCB through Professional Identity and Intrinsic Motivation. In contrast, the hypothesized Material Rewards pathways through Professional Identity and Extrinsic Motivation were not supported. These findings extend hospitality motivation research by highlighting the importance of identity-affirming managerial practices in frontline service settings.

Railway signaling software must satisfy strict requirements—clarity, completeness, verifiability, and traceability—from the specification phase. KRS-SG-0069 requirements are written in Korean natural language, making manual structuring costly and expert-dependent. I propose a semi-automated framework combining LLM-based structuring with deterministic verification. Analysis of 94 requirements identified seven defect types mapped to EN 50128 clause 7.2.4 violations. The framework comprises four modules: M1 classifies requirements; M2 converts them into a six-element boilerplate via Chain-of-Thought prompting; M3 validates drafts through a four-layer rule engine; M4 generates state transition models, test cases, and a traceability matrix. The LLM is confined to draft generation, while safety judgments are delegated to deterministic engines and formal validators. This paper presents an architectural foundation; quantitative evaluation and broader applicability remain as future work.

The paper offers a theoretical and analytical substantiation of the psychological features of the interrelation between occupational stress and emotional burnout of academic staff at Ukrainian higher education institutions working under the full-scale war. Several interrelated circumstances make the issue pressing. First, the work of a university teacher belongs to the "person-to-person" socionomic professions characterised by chronic emotional load, whereby prolonged exposure to stressors regularly develops into burnout. Second, war-related factors – a permanent threat to life, forced displacement, institutional relocation, distance and blended learning, power and communication disruptions – are superimposed on the "ordinary" academic stressors and greatly intensify them. Third, longitudinal observations reveal not an episodic but a progressive increase of burnout among Ukrainian teachers: the share of persons with a high level of emotional exhaustion rose from 49.5 % in July 2022 to 71.8 % in January 2024. Analysis of current scholarly sources – recent professional publications of 2023–2025, analytical reports and official statistics – made it possible to order the phenomenology of the "stress – burnout" link in the war context and to reveal the mechanism of transition from the former to the latter. The meanings of "occupational stress" and "emotional burnout syndrome" are clarified, the two are distinguished, and the genetic connection between them is shown. War stressors of a teacher are systematised into three groups – existential-security, organisational-professional, and communicative-emotional. A theoretical model of the stress–burnout interrelation is built, in which coping strategies, psychological resourcefulness and institutional support act as the key mediating links. A three-level system of burnout prevention – individual, group and institutional – is proposed together with a list of concrete measures. The materials obtained can be applied directly when designing programmes of psychological support for academic staff, planning measures to preserve their occupational health and making managerial decisions at the level of a higher education institution.

The article examines the mechanisms of public administration for ensuring the quality of higher education in Ukraine through the prism of the classifications established in the scholarly discourse, as well as through the practices of their functioning and their actual impact on the international competitiveness of domestic higher education institutions. The methodological basis of the research combines the analysis of regulatory and legal acts, programme documents of the international and national levels, statistical data of the National Agency for Higher Education Quality Assurance, and a comparative analysis of the dynamics of the positioning of Ukrainian universities in the leading international rankings during 2022–2026. A contradiction has been identified between the architectonics of building the higher education quality assurance system and the comparatively low positioning of Ukrainian universities in international rankings (Quacquarelli Symonds World University Rankings; Times Higher Education World University Rankings; Academic Ranking of World Universities, ShanghaiRanking). In particular, it has been established that the number of Ukrainian universities represented in the QS World University Rankings decreased from 11 in 2023 to 4 in 2026, while the highest position of domestic institutions in the Times Higher Education ranking has consistently remained within the 801–1000 group despite the quantitative growth of their representation. The exhaustion of the potential of the traditional regulatory-legal, organisational- administrative and economic mechanisms of public administration in the higher education sphere has been substantiated, along with the need to search for new mechanisms of public administration for ensuring quality. The article also offers proposals on the necessity of applying innovative mechanisms for ensuring the quality of higher education, namely those grounded in the toolkit of artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and robotic process automation, the practical significance of which is confirmed by international experience and the analytical priorities of the national quality assurance system.
topics: Education and Social Development in Ukraine

documents.abstract: Higher education plays a pivotal role in shaping a nation's economic growth, technological advancement, and social development. India possesses one of the world's largest higher education systems, comprising over one thousand universities and thousands of colleges that collectively educate millions of students annually. Despite significant expansion in institutional capacity and enrolment over the past two decades, maintaining quality remains a major concern. Challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, faculty shortages, disparities in access, limited research productivity, employability gaps, insufficient industry-academia collaboration, governance issues, and unequal digital access continue to impede the realization of globally competitive higher education. Simultaneously, transformative initiatives including the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, digital learning platforms, research funding reforms, international collaborations, multidisciplinary education, and the integration of artificial intelligence present unprecedented opportunities for systemic improvement. This review critically examines the current status of higher education quality in India by synthesizing evidence from government reports, policy documents, and contemporary scholarly literature. The paper discusses the multidimensional challenges affecting educational quality and evaluates emerging opportunities driven by technological innovation, quality assurance mechanisms, competency-based curricula, and global academic partnerships. Furthermore, it proposes strategic recommendations to strengthen governance, faculty development, research ecosystems, institutional autonomy, accreditation, digital transformation, and employability. The study concludes that achieving sustainable excellence in higher education requires coordinated efforts among policymakers, regulatory agencies, academic institutions, industry, and society. A learner-centric, technology-enabled, research-oriented, and globally connected higher education system will be fundamental to realizing India's vision of becoming a global knowledge economy by 2047.

ABSTRACT Electrochemical advanced oxidation processes (EAOPs) have become a prominent tool in wastewater remediation of refractory organic pollutants due to their versatility and ability to generate powerful, in situ oxidant species—predominantly hydroxyl radicals (•OH). Concurrently, quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models have emerged as vital tools for predicting activity in high‐priority areas like drug development and toxicity. In this review, we address the application of QSARs in decoding reactivity within electrooxidation processes. We trace their evolution from early origins using the Hammett parameter () as a molecular descriptor to quantum chemical descriptors—such as , ionization potentials (IPs), and Fukui functions—and finally to advanced machine learning (ML) approaches like graph neural networks (GNNs) designed to navigate complex real wastewater matrices. Additionally, we highlight the anode as a core mechanistic variable that dictates oxidant selectivity. Finally, we discuss the primary limitations hindering ML adoption in EAOPs—including small training sets, a lack of electrochemical‐specific datasets, limited water‐matrix transferability, black‐box interpretability, and conflicting optimization metrics—and explore emerging strategies to overcome them, such as transfer learning, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and physics‐informed ML.

This volume examines one of the most important teacher–scholar projects of our time: innovating pedagogies and ethics in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). The volume brings together scholarship in three sections: Introductions, Digital Agency and Giving Students Voice, and Embodied Pedagogies. In this volume, we curate scholarship that engages with pedagogical governance for educators, digital storytelling, inclusive pedagogy, discussion boards, online student engagement, autoethnography, documentary-making, ecological consciousness, study practices, community-centered learning, and Geographic Information System (GIS) mapping. Taken together, this body of research demonstrates that meaningful learning is not only cognitive but also emotional, relational, and contextual, which requires pedagogies that attend to empathy, belonging, and lived experience. Across diverse contexts, educators are provided with pedagogical tools to support students in developing critical thinking and reflection skills while also fostering social responsibility and a commitment to the common good. All these elements are essential to this timely, interdisciplinary teacher–scholar project to support ethical AI in education.

Analytical chemistry plays an essential role in the identification, separation, quantification, and characterization of pharmaceutical substances. Recent technological developments have introduced advanced analytical approaches with improved sensitivity, accuracy, selectivity, speed, and reliability.[1] This review focuses on recent research in chromatography, mass spectrometry, spectroscopy, biosensors, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML), and Green Analytical Chemistry. Modern chromatographic and mass spectrometric techniques enable efficient separation, structural characterization, impurity profiling, and sensitive analysis of complex samples. Spectroscopic techniques provide rapid and non-destructive characterization, while biosensors offer sensitive, rapid, and potentially portable detection systems. AI/ML approaches are increasingly applied for analytical data processing, prediction, pattern recognition, and method optimization. Green analytical approaches aim to minimize hazardous solvents, waste generation, energy consumption, and sample requirements while maintaining analytical performance.[2] The review compares the methodologies, major findings, strengths, limitations, and research gaps reported in recent studies. Overall, the integration of advanced instrumentation, intelligent data analysis, biosensing technologies, and sustainable analytical practices is expected to contribute to the development of faster, more sensitive, reliable, automated, and environmentally sustainable pharmaceutical analytical methods.

Caries risk assessment (CRA) is intended to estimate an individual's likelihood of developing new caries lesions or experiencing lesion progression over a defined period so that preventive, diagnostic and recall strategies can be tailored. Contemporary CRA is changing rapidly. Established approaches such as Cariogram, Caries Management by Risk Assessment (CAMBRA), professional checklists and risk-based care pathways are increasingly being supplemented by statistical prediction models, machine learning, digital self-assessment, salivary and microbiome biomarkers, and population-specific tools. This critical narrative review evaluates whether these developments have improved prognosis rather than merely increased technical complexity. Literature published principally from 2015 to 8 August 2026 was examined, while earlier seminal studies were retained when necessary to establish concepts and validation history. The synthesis distinguishes future-event prediction from cross-sectional detection or classification, because this distinction is frequently blurred in the recent literature. The strongest and most reproducible conventional predictor remains previous or current caries experience, while social conditions, fluoride exposure, plaque, diet, salivary function and life-course factors modify risk. Established multifactorial tools can structure clinical reasoning and risk-linked care, but external validation remains uneven and evidence that their use itself improves patient outcomes is limited. Machine-learning studies often report promising discrimination, yet many rely on cross-sectional outcomes, internal validation, small samples or incomplete calibration and clinical-utility assessment. Prospective cohorts demonstrate that simple, readily collected predictors can perform competitively, challenging assumptions that algorithmic complexity necessarily improves care. Salivary, microbiome and genetic approaches remain biologically informative but are not yet sufficiently standardised or externally validated for routine prognostic use. The most important recent trend is therefore methodological rather than technological: CRA is moving towards explicit prediction horizons, transparent validation, calibration, decision-linked utility, population transportability and repeated reassessment. Future progress will depend on prospective multicentre validation and impact studies that compare complex models against parsimonious clinical baselines and test whether risk-guided decisions improve outcomes without widening inequalities.

Generative AI is reshaping video production from a set of isolated tools into a core production infrastructure. This chapter presents an integrative value-chain framework showing how AI transforms pre-production, production, post-production, and distribution. It identifies four major shifts: workflow compression, creative augmentation, scale and personalization, and disintermediation. The chapter also examines the tension between democratization, in which low-cost AI tools empower small studios, educators, and creators in emerging economies, and consolidation, in which powerful firms control foundation models, compute, data, and distribution. Using cases on virtual production, AI-assisted localization, and the 2023 Hollywood labor agreements, it discusses key governance issues, including labor displacement, intellectual property disputes, content authenticity, and audience trust. It argues that AI is reorganizing video production as an economic system and offers recommendations for scholars, practitioners, and policymakers, especially in the Global South.

Safety-aligned language models are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining useful for benign ones. However, because many evaluations score only the final response, they often conflate intent understanding with response-level safety behavior. To address this, we introduce RiskCueBench, a recoverability-controlled benchmark that separates these two stages by first measuring whether a model can successfully recover a high-level intent and then evaluating its safety behavior on the same prompt. RiskCueBench contains 160 latent intents and 640 abstract non-operational surface prompts across eight risk categories. The benchmark covers 25 completed model groups and 32,000 successful model outputs with final rubric-adjudicated labels. When conditioning on pairs where both surface forms are recoverable, we find that increased contextualized specificity induces a shift toward less safe behavior. Specifically, paired bootstrap estimates show that the refusal rate and global safety score decrease by 0.175 and 0.440, respectively. Furthermore, mixed effects modeling corroborates a 0.107 increase in unsafe cooperation. These results show that the safety behavior can be miscalibrated to the surface form even after the intent has been recovered, motivating safety evaluations that report response behavior conditional on semantic recoverability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This reflective article identifies three interconnected themes for advancing scholarship on new technology, work and employment. First, it calls for stronger theorisation of technology and deeper engagement with the political economy of Big Tech and AI. Attending to the material and political dimensions of technological systems is vital for challenging dominant narratives that present technologically driven change as inevitable. Second, the article argues for widening the empirical scope of research beyond the “new, new technologies,” while overlooking less visible sectors and the differing experiences of adopters and non‐adopters within the same industries. Broadening the empirical field and methodological repertoire would illuminate the uneven and variegated nature of digitalisation. Third, the article emphasises the importance of historical contextualisation. Situating contemporary developments within longer trajectories of workplace transformation is essential for understanding ongoing challenges and informing research on work futures.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

LLM safety evaluations via jailbreaking typically index on attack success rate (ASR): whether a generated response violates safeguards. However, ASR only evaluates sampled outputs and provides little information on the underlying generation process. Autoregressive language models define distributions over possible outputs, and a sampled refusal can coexist with substantial probability mass on harmful generation paths. We study this hidden structure through bounded continuation analysis (BCA), which models autoregressive generation as a stochastic process over token prefixes and computes the finite-horizon probability that generation reaches a harmful continuation. BCA constructs a bounded continuation tree, labels terminal continuations with a semantic harm evaluator, and estimates harmful reachability using exact probabilistic model checking. BCA complements ASR by measuring how much harmful behavior remains accessible beneath a sampled safe response. This makes it useful for distinguishing models that look identical under measured ASR values, and allocating red-team effort toward regions of the generation process with greater hidden risk. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and 100 JailbreakBench behaviors, we show that BCA effectively quantifies hidden harmful behavior and provides a useful signal to guide red teaming.

The worldwide demand for nutraceuticals and herbal products has grown rapidly due to their growing role in health promotion and disease prevention.Despite their widespread use, regulatory approaches differ substantially among countries, leading to inconsistencies in product quality, safety evaluation, and international commercialization.This review examines and compares the regulatory systems of the United States, the European Union, India, Japan, China, Canada, and Australia, with particular attention to product classification, marketing authorization, quality assurance, raw material standardisation, and post-market monitoring.Evidence from published reports was also assessed to identify the consequences of regulatory gaps.The analysis indicates that differences in regulatory expectations contribute to problems such as adulteration, contamination, incorrect botanical identification, and inconsistent product performance.Well-documented incidents, including Aristolochia-induced nephropathy, cardiovascular events linked to Ephedra-containing products, liver injury associated with Hydroxycut, and heavy metal contamination in certain Ayurvedic preparations, demonstrate the potential health risks arising from inadequate regulatory control.The findings emphasize the need for greater international alignment of regulatory practices, stronger standards for raw material quality, improved surveillance throughout the product lifecycle, and the adoption of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence to strengthen regulatory decision-making while accommodating country-specific regulatory frameworks.

As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.

ABSTRACT Background The ceramic industry is an important component of Iran’s manufacturing sector; however, its complex production processes can generate respirable crystalline silica (RCS), a well-established occupational hazard associated with adverse respiratory outcomes. Objectives This study aimed to characterize RCS exposure levels, assess associated occupational health risks, and evaluate pulmonary function among ceramic workers in Iran. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among ceramic workers using a Similar Exposure Group (SEG) approach. A total of 79 personal respirable dust samples were collected across seven production tasks. RCS concentrations were determined according to NIOSH Method 7601 using a JENWAY 6105 UV/Visible spectrophotometer. Deterministic health risk assessment and Monte Carlo simulation (1,000 iterations) were performed based on the U.S. EPA methodology. Pulmonary function was assessed using spirometry, including forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV 1 ), forced vital capacity (FVC), and the FEV 1 /FVC ratio. Associations between RCS exposure and pulmonary function parameters were evaluated statistically. Results Mean RCS concentrations varied substantially across production tasks, ranging from 0.02 mg/m 3 in glazing operations to 0.50 mg/m 3 in crushing operations. Exposure levels among crusher workers and ball-mill spray operators significantly exceeded the occupational exposure limit of 0.025 mg/m 3 (p < 0.05). Deterministic risk assessment yielded hazard quotient (HQ) values below 1; however, Monte Carlo simulation showed that the 95th percentile HQ slightly exceeded 1, indicating an increased non-carcinogenic risk under high-exposure scenarios. Spirometric results were predominantly within normal ranges, although borderline obstructive and restrictive patterns were observed among packing and furnace workers. Significant negative correlations were observed between RCS concentration and FEV 1 (r s = −0.77, p = 0.04) and the FEV 1 /FVC ratio (r s = −0.78, p = 0.03). Conclusions Ceramic workers, particularly those involved in crushing and ball-mill operations, may experience substantial RCS exposure and increased respiratory health risks. The observed associations between RCS exposure and reduced pulmonary function highlight the need for effective engineering controls, respiratory protection programs, routine exposure monitoring, and periodic medical surveillance to reduce occupational health risks in the ceramic industry.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organisational decision-making, creating opportunities for innovation and sustainability while intensifying concerns about accountability, transparency, stakeholder responsibility and human oversight. This structured theory-building integrative review synthesises a purposively bounded corpus of 35 unique works on responsible AI, AI governance, responsible leadership and organisational sustainability. Responsible AI Governance (RAIG) is conceptualised as a multidimensional organisational capability: the repeatable, coordinated and adaptive capacity through which responsible AI principles are translated into governance structures, decision processes, accountability arrangements, stakeholder relationships, human oversight and assurance across the AI lifecycle. Six interdependent dimensions are specified: ethical-strategic alignment, accountability architecture, human oversight and agency, stakeholder inclusion, transparency and assurance and lifecycle governance and adaptability. Responsible leadership is positioned as an antecedent managerial microfoundation rather than a constitutive dimension of RAIG. The framework separates sustainability from the content of RAIG and theorises sustainable organisational and stakeholder outcomes as consequences of effective governance. Propositions and a staged research programme establish a foundation for construct operationalisation, cross-context validation and subsequent nomological testing.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence now shapes digital marketing, influencing targeting, personalization, pricing, content creation, and customer engagement. However, its use creates risks including algorithmic bias, personalization–privacy tensions, manipulative interface design, and declining consumer trust following AI disclosure. This chapter addresses a gap by integrating these risks with the design and governance mechanisms needed for responsible AI in digital marketing. Drawing on research in marketing, information systems, public administration, and law, it examines algorithmic risk, consumer trust, explainability, transparency, governance, and regulation. The review identifies consumer trust as the key mechanism linking algorithmic risk to marketing outcomes and proposes an integrated framework in which fairness auditing, consent-based data practices, responsible interface design, and explainability act as design levers, while governance and regulation establish implementation conditions. The chapter argues that responsible AI can help manage algorithmic risk and build trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming digital marketing by enabling automation and personalization. For micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), AI offers opportunities to enhance competitiveness despite limited resources. However, adoption introduces risks such as privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, and cybersecurity threats that may undermine customer trust. These challenges are especially critical in emerging economies facing financial and technical constraints. The primary objective of this chapter is to systematically investigate the intersection of AI and digital marketing strategies among MSMEs in Oman, aligning responsible practices with Oman Vision 2040. Employing a qualitative, conceptual desk research methodology built on a systematic literature review, this study applies Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE), Trust, and Stakeholder frameworks to identify operational barriers and propose a sustainable growth framework centered on transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy, and human oversight.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: As generative AI tools rapidly integrate into higher education—assisting with instruction, content generation, student evaluation, and research—universities face a complex landscape of ethical challenges. Drawing on a detailed review of current scholarship, this study evaluates the integration of generative AI, focusing on ongoing debates surrounding academic integrity, authorship, and the reliability of machine-generated output. Beyond individual misconduct, it addresses broader systemic risks, including algorithmic bias, data privacy vulnerabilities, detector inaccuracies, and the urgent need for clear institutional governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are rapidly reshaping university learning environments, yet pedagogical and ethical frameworks have not developed at the same pace as their adoption. Adopting a multidisciplinary approach, this study combines empirical evidence from a survey of 117 undergraduate Engineering and Health Sciences students with the pedagogical perspectives of university lecturers. It examines how students currently use GenAI and how these tools can be meaningfully integrated into teaching and learning. Findings show that students’ first exposure to GenAI is mainly driven by informal social media channels rather than institutional guidance, resulting in uneven and often unguided adoption. The study also identifies a “contradictory profile” in 11% of the sample: students who perceive GenAI use as a form of cheating while also expressing a strong demand for formal training on its academic integration. From the lecturers’ perspective, GenAI offers opportunities to support content creation, assessment design, and instructional workflows, provided that human-led teaching remains central. By integrating observed student behaviors with expert recommendations, this research proposes an ethical framework and practical guidelines for the responsible integration of GenAI in higher education. The study highlights the urgent need for institutional policies that address emerging socio-ethical tensions and ensure that GenAI enhances, rather than circumvents, foundational knowledge, academic integrity, and critical thinking.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Revolutionizing Tertiary Education for Africa's Thriving AI Economy and Workforce (RetAIn) project presents a comprehensive, multi-method investigation into the conditions, constraints, and catalysts shaping Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption across African Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Deploying both qualitative multi-stakeholders Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) from three African countries (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia) and a quantitative cross-country survey across five Sub-Saharan African nations (Ghana, Rwanda, Namibia, Kenya, and Zambia), this study produces a richly triangulated account of AI integration dynamics on the continent. The FGD strand revealed a stark divergence in national AI trajectories: Rwanda operates under a strong top-down policy vision hindered by institutional rigidity; Namibia exhibits pragmatic institutional adaptability constrained by geographic and economic smallness; and Ghana demonstrates emergent, bottom-up innovation within a national policy vacuum. The survey strand, drawing on 156 responses across five countries, corroborated these qualitative tensions, documenting widespread recognition of AI's strategic importance alongside limited structured engagement, persistent infrastructure deficits, and marked equity barriers, particularly for women, vulnerable groups, rural students, and part-time workers. From both methods, a unifying finding emerges: AI integration in African HEIs consistently fails when technical adoption outpaces social, pedagogical, and governance co-evolution. The study argues for context-specific, socio-technically grounded strategies that pair curriculum co-design with robust industry partnerships, that centre equity and cultural relevance, and build governance frameworks capable of guiding, rather than chasing, technological change.

Modern translator training faces a structural mismatch: technology is typically taught as a set of isolated modules, one tool per topic, while professional translation practice treats these same tools as an interconnected workflow in which a single instrument routinely performs functions attributed to several distinct stages. This article reframes the transla- tion process as a technological chain comprising four interrelated components – pre-translation analysis, CAT-assisted translation supported by an AI agent, quality management, and file preparation – and argues that these components are better represented as a network of overlapping actions than as a linear sequence of self-contained stages. Drawing on both theoretical models of translator competence (PACTE’s instrumental competence, the EMT framework) and empirical studies of specific tools and stages, the article identifies a gap between well-established theoretical support for cross- cutting technical competence and its still-fragmented empirical and classroom validation. The study demonstrates, through classroom examples – including the pre-editing of auto-generated video subtitles using regular expressions and a compar- ative analysis of PDF-document translation across several CAT environments – that a single technological action routinely crosses the boundaries between the four proposed stages, undermining the pedagogical logic of modular instruction. The article proposes a network model of the translation technological chain, in which the four components function as condi- tional nodes connected by feedback and cross-cutting links rather than fixed sequential order, and grounds this model in the broader concept of a translator’s digital literacy. The findings support a concrete pedagogical principle: technical com- petence formation should be organized around cross-cutting, project-based assignments that require students to move across several nodes of the model, rather than around isolated tool-specific modules. The article concludes by identifying directions for further research, including the applicability of the proposed model to team-based translation workflows and an unresolved gap between the documented professional importance of quality-management tools and students’ compar- atively modest perception of their value.

Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. We develop a conversational multi-agent system called ReviewPilot that automates the PRISMA workflow from paper screening to information extraction. Researchers can tailor criteria and schemas through dialogue, and a project memory keeps their configurations and revisions. Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source. On epidemiological expert reviews, ReviewPilot outperforms a single-prompt LLM and AgentSLR across three LLMs, with screening macro F1 up to 0.776 and extraction F1 up to 0.788. Case studies in biomedicine and human-computer interaction show close agreement with human annotators, suggesting that ReviewPilot can transfer beyond epidemiology. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/ReviewPilot.

Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.

documents.abstract: This chapter aims to explore the intricate relationship between authenticity, trust, and consumer loyalty in influencer marketing. Authenticity is pivotal in influencer marketing, where consumers, inundated with curated content, crave honesty and relatable experiences. Genuine passion from influencers for brands builds trust and transparency, connecting brands with consumers. This connection fosters positive brand perceptions and purchase intent.. By demystifying the role of authenticity in influencer marketing, this chapter aims to empower brands to circumnavigate the digital landscape effectively and build genuine relationships with their target audiences. Ultimately, it pursues to underwrite to a more transparent and trustworthy influencer marketing environment that benefits both consumers and brands. However, the advent of AI Technology and the rapid progress in this field have helped marketers to identify these challenges and solve their inherent problems. Also, AI today truly provides new and exciting avenues for marketing companies.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are redefining how people access and navigate community healthcare. Concurrently, community nursing services are facing a sustained workforce decline. While digital nurse leadership has matured in many acute organisations, community nurses are increasingly expected to deliver technology-enabled care without equivalent leadership structures, support or career pathways. In this article, the author details a proposal for a digital specialist community public health nurse (digital SCPHN) role framework. The author describes the digital SCPHN as first and foremost a clinician, with digital capability as an essential enhancement rather than a replacement of core nursing objectives. Positioned as a digital translator and champion within community teams, the digital SCPHN helps people to navigate complex digital healthcare systems while supporting their colleagues through technology-enabled care prioritisation, secure safeguarding communication and community risk insight. The author also outlines six actionable recommendations for front-line nurses, team leads and system commissioners to strengthen community nursing impact, improve digital literacy and ensure equitable, person-centred care in digitally enabled neighbourhood healthcare systems.

Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal $p$-values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.

topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Knowing the layout of the physical world matters for many applications, yet the sensors we rely on for it (e.g., cameras and LiDAR) can fail in darkness, in adverse weather, or behind walls. Wireless signals do not face these limitations: every link between a base station and a user is shaped by the buildings it passes, reflects from, or is blocked by, leaving information about the surrounding scene embedded in the wireless channel measured at the endpoints. However, mapping channel measurements to the environment is a severely ill-posed problem: a measurement records only the structures that interact with the transmitted electromagnetic waves along its propagation paths, and even these observations can often be explained by multiple plausible scenes. We therefore formulate wireless scene reconstruction as posterior inference and develop a hierarchical framework with two complementary stages to approach this problem. A wireless foundation model, pretrained to respect propagation physics, transforms each channel measurement into a representation of the scene structure that shaped the observation. A diffusion model then jointly integrates representations from multiple measurements to model and sample the posterior over building occupancy, with consensus over samples producing the final reconstruction. We demonstrate that the framework can accurately recover building footprints from wireless channel measurements alone and show that its performance depends critically on both design components: physics-grounded representations expose scene-relevant information, while joint posterior inference coherently integrates complementary observations.

Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$Π$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$Π$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.

documents.abstract: This working paper constitutes the first deliverable under the EFSA contract RTD/2023/OP/0011 – Lot 1 on Foresight on Demand in Science, Technology, Research and Innovation Policy, implemented within the framework of multi-agency foresight on One Health and authorised by the European Commission, DG Research & Innovation, G1 – Common R&I Strategy and Foresight Service. It examines the relevance of the One Health approach for a broad range of European institutions and agencies and argues that One Health has become an increasingly important framework for addressing the complex and interdependent challenges facing the European Union. These challenges include emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental pollution, climate change, food insecurity, mental health pressures, and widening social inequalities, all of which cut across traditional sectoral and institutional boundaries. The report situates One Health within its broader conceptual and policy context. It shows that the approach has evolved from earlier biomedical understandings centred on zoonotic disease and veterinary-public health cooperation into a wider framework linking human, animal, plant, and environmental health. In line with the recommendations of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, the report adopts the OHHLEP definition of One Health as an integrated and unifying approach aimed at balancing and optimizing the health of humans, animals, plants, and ecosystems. At the same time, it underlines that important ambiguities remain concerning the interpretation, scope, and operationalisation of the concept, especially in the context of European governance. The report therefore not only maps One Health as a thematic field but also examines how it can serve as a practical basis for stronger coordination among EU agencies and institutions. A central finding is that One Health is already relevant to a wide constellation of EU bodies, even if this relevance is not always explicitly recognised or institutionally coordinated. The report highlights the roles of DG SANTE, DG ENV, DG CLIMA, DG AGRI, and the Joint Research Centre, as well as agencies such as EFSA, EMA, ECDC, EEA, ECHA, EUDA, EU-OSHA, Frontex, EIGE, and ETF. These actors contribute complementary expertise across food safety, infectious disease monitoring, environmental protection, chemical safety, medicines regulation, occupational health, social inequalities, and preparedness. The report notes that cooperation has already advanced through initiatives such as the ONE Conference, the cross-agency One Health task force, and joint work on zoonoses and antimicrobial resistance. However, it also finds that collaboration remains uneven, fragmented, and often dependent on issue-specific rather than strategic coordination. Existing efforts show strong potential, but the absence of a fully integrated governance architecture continues to limit the EU’s capacity to translate One Health into a genuinely shared and anticipatory policy framework. On this basis, the report develops a broad and integrated overview of the main scientific themes currently shaping the One Health agenda. These include infectious diseases and health security, veterinary medical products, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental and climate-related health risks, animal health and welfare, public health and disease prevention, sustainable food systems, inequalities and governance, digitalisation and health, and education and training. A major contribution of the report is that it expands the One Health agenda beyond its more established focus on zoonoses and AMR. It argues that issues such as chemical pollution, microplastics, PFAS, unsafe food systems, occupational health, illicit drugs, mental health, militarization, nuclear risks, and the health implications of geopolitical change must also be considered within a One Health framework because they arise from and reinforce the interdependence of environmental, animal, and human health. The report therefore presents One Health not as a narrow technical field, but as a broader framework for understanding and governing systemic and interacting risks. The report also emphasizes that the One Health perspective is closely aligned with broader EU strategic priorities. It shows that One Health contributes not only to public health protection, but also to goals related to sustainable prosperity, food security, preparedness, climate resilience, social fairness, and democratic legitimacy. In this sense, One Health is framed as a governance approach capable of linking prevention, resilience, and sustainability across domains that are too often treated separately. The report repeatedly stresses that challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, environmental degradation, food insecurity, and health inequalities cannot be addressed adequately through isolated policy responses. Rather, they require integrated surveillance, coordinated foresight, and stronger institutional mechanisms capable of connecting evidence, preparedness, and action across sectors and scales. A further important conclusion is that One Health must be treated as both a scientific and institutional innovation agenda. The report identifies the need for stronger inter- and transdisciplinary collaboration, improved data sharing, harmonised surveillance systems, and clearer coordination mechanisms at EU level. It supports the view that the European Union should adopt a more coherent One Health strategy, backed by adequate resources, shared infrastructures, and long-term political support. Education and training are also identified as crucial pillars. One Health concepts should be integrated into academic, professional, and public learning environments, while digital tools, artificial intelligence, and data systems should be developed in line with ethical, inclusive, and sustainable principles. At the same time, the report warns that digitalisation, if poorly governed, may reproduce inequalities, deepen data divides, and generate new environmental burdens. In its final section, the report moves from thematic mapping to strategic foresight. It identifies a series of emerging and cross-cutting areas that merit particular attention in future collaboration. These include cross-border health threats and joint preparedness, chemicals and environmental exposures, illicit drugs and their environmental and social dimensions, climate change and health inequalities, social determinants of health, mental health, digitalisation, and militarization. Across all these areas, the report underscores the need for strengthened multi-agency collaboration and more systematic data sharing. It argues that the EU already possesses many of the institutional building blocks required for a stronger One Health approach, but that these assets need to be connected more effectively through coordinated foresight, shared analytical tools, and common strategic priorities. Overall, the report presents One Health as a necessary and forward-looking framework for European governance. It shows that the health of people, animals, plants, and ecosystems is increasingly shaped by interconnected pressures that no single institution, sector, or Member State can manage alone. By embedding One Health more firmly in research agendas, legislative initiatives, surveillance systems, education, and inter-agency cooperation, the European Union can improve its capacity to anticipate and respond to multidimensional threats while also advancing sustainability, equity, and resilience. In this sense, One Health is not merely a conceptual lens, but a practical foundation for future European collaboration in science, regulation, and strategic policy development.

documents.abstract: Understanding how the human brain constructs meaning from real-world language remains a fundamental challenge, as semantics depend on context that varies in natural settings. To enable the study of real-world linguistic meaning in the brain, we introduce SCRIBE, a framework grounded in a neuroscience-informed semantic space that leverages an ensemble of open-source large language models to generate interpretable, word-level semantic representations of arbitrary text. In a behavioral study with 921 participants, we show that human semantic feature judgments vary systematically with context, and that SCRIBE captures these shifts, reaching 75-81% of the estimated human noise ceiling. Using brain activity recorded while participants listen to naturalistic stories, we further demonstrate that SCRIBE predicts neural responses in language-selective brain regions, significantly outperforming non-contextual semantic representations. Variance partitioning reveals that SCRIBE explains unique brain-predictive information beyond syntactic features, suggesting that its representations capture aspects of linguistic meaning not accounted for by the measured syntactic features. Together, these findings establish SCRIBE as a scalable and interpretable foundation for studying natural language semantics in the brain.

With the advent of Internet of Things technologies and intelligent edge computing systems, the surface of cyber-attacks has been increasingly growing, which results in the problem of network security in distributed systems. This chapter will provide a review of intelligent intrusion detection methods using AI for secure intelligent edge ecosystems in the IoT. The chapter will discuss how machine learning, deep learning, and federated learning models are used together with edge computing systems to increase detection accuracy, reduce the time needed for detection, and maintain scalability while preserving data privacy. Furthermore, the proposed framework takes into account explainable artificial intelligence, privacy-preserving learning, and deployment techniques to overcome problems related to limited resource constraints of edge devices. Also, this chapter explores present security issues, application scenarios, implementation issues, and future perspectives, such as zero trust architecture, collaborative edge intelligence, and autonomous cyber defense systems.

Abstract Query optimization is a crucial problem in database systems that has been studied for decades. Learned query optimizers (LQOs) can improve performance over time by incorporating feedback; however, they suffer from cold-start issues and often require retraining when workloads shift or schemas change. We initially proposed SEFRQO, a Self-Evolving Fine-tuned RAG-based Query Optimizer, which leverages fine-tuned LLMs to address these challenges and uses in-context learning to achieve continuous evolution. However, its system design relies on the assumption of repetitive query workloads, requires executing queries statically upon their first encounter (incurring extra overhead), and utilizes only partial feedback from the best historical records (insufficient feedback design). In this paper, we present SEFRQO-Plus, which resolves the above limitations. First, we design a feedback-oriented vector database with query structure-aware embeddings to support effective similarity search, and we incorporate multi-layered histories as references to enrich the feedback. Then, we enhance the prompt optimization workflow by utilizing multi-dimensional historical feedback to drive continuous self-evolution. Moreover, we provide formal theoretical proofs to validate the advantages of our customized query group relative policy optimization. Evaluations show that SEFRQO-Plus outperforms state-of-the-art LQOs, achieving reductions of 66.52% and 69.79% in query latency for the complete CEB and Stack workloads, respectively, compared to PostgreSQL. SEFRQO-Plus achieves an additional 15% improvement over the initial SEFRQO. Moreover, it generalizes effectively across multiple workloads and scenarios, and even across different DBMSes.

Abstract Background In recent years, the availability of digital therapeutic apps in medicine, digital therapeutics (DTx), has significantly increased. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of DTx, an increasing number of scientific studies have been conducted in this field. Several authors have pointed out that a standardized approach to DTx evaluation is relevant to improving the comparability of apps in the future. Currently, it is unclear how study authors proceed when selecting outcomes and measurement methods (O&M) for DTx studies. Objective The primary aim of this study was to investigate how study authors currently select O&M in DTx studies, specifically for applications delivered in the form of apps. The secondary objectives were to collect suggestions for improving the comparability of DTx apps and studies in the future and to examine whether core outcome sets (COS) could represent a possible solution for enhancing comparability. Methods This study was based on 19 semistructured interviews. All interview partners had prior experience in planning and conducting DTx studies. The interviews were conducted between August 2024 and November 2024. Subsequently, qualitative data analysis was performed according to Kuckartz and Rädiker using a deductive-inductive research approach. Results The results of this study showed that the methodological approach for selecting O&M in DTx studies was primarily based on research, as well as on personal prior experience and individual ideas. Interview participants indicated that when selecting O&M, they particularly focused on aspects such as scientific quality criteria or practical implementation and feasibility. A suggestion for achieving better comparability of DTx studies in the future was to use standardized O&M per therapeutic indication area. Almost all interviewees considered COS to be a suitable approach for improving the comparability of DTx and associated studies. However, we also identified critical perspectives that questioned their application. Conclusions Across professional groups, both commonalities and differences were observed in methodological approaches as well as in the selection of O&M in DTx studies. To improve the comparability of DTx interventions and trials, several approaches have been developed, for example, through the use of guidance frameworks, artificial intelligence programs, or the establishment of COS. However, further research is warranted to advance this field.

The emergence of the artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) has led to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. For many of these threats, labeled training data are scarce or unavailable, which increases the need for label-free intrusion detection systems. To address this issue, this study proposes a self-supervised one-class TabNet framework, termed SS-OC-TabNet, for intrusion detection in tabular network traffic. The framework combines self-supervised representation learning and one-class compactness learning within a two-stage training process. In the first stage, masked-feature reconstruction is used to learn the feature structure of normal traffic from unlabeled data. In the second stage, a hypersphere compactness objective is applied to make the latent representations of normal traffic more compact for anomaly detection. TabNet is used as the backbone to support sequential feature selection, which also improves interpretability. The proposed model was evaluated on the NSL-KDD dataset and further validated through comparison with related works on the ToN-IoT dataset, achieving an accuracy of 93.20% with a false alarm rate of 2.13%. Further, the interpretability results show which traffic features influence the model's decisions. The compact design and low computational complexity of the proposed framework also support energy-efficient deployment in resource-constrained AIoT environments. These results indicate that SS-OC-TabNet is a viable tool for label-free intrusion detection in AIoT environments. documents.abstract: Studies suggest that computer workers may benefit from cycling workstations; however, little is known about the sex-specific mechanistic impacts of cycling on computer work-related risk factors. Twenty-six computer users (14 females) underwent two 60-min sessions of typing: one sitting, and one lightly cycling, while performance, symptoms and electromyography were recorded. Results show that males' typing speed was lower during cycling than sitting, while females' performance remained similar between conditions (Sex × Condition, p = 0.029). Neck/shoulder and visual discomfort were lower during cycling for both sexes, with females experiencing less neck/shoulder discomfort than males (Sex × Condition × Time, p = 0.006). Neck/shoulder muscle activation increased with time during sitting but decreased during cycling, especially in females. Low back muscle activity was higher during cycling, particularly in females (Sex × Condition × Time interaction, p = 0.046). Findings suggest sex-specific responses to cycling during computer work.

This study examines collaborative learning design with a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) co-pilot among in-service university English teachers in China. In a between-subjects experiment ( N = 60), epistemic network analysis (ENA) was used to model the situated discourse structures of team dialogues, complemented by thematic analysis of interviews. AI-supported teams achieved higher overall scores on a rubric covering constructive alignment, Universal Design for Learning principles, and other aspects of learning design. ENA identified task-specific differences in collaborative discourse, with AI-supported teams displaying a more interconnected and learner-centered network. Participants described the AI as a pedagogical conscience and an intellectual sparring partner whose prompts kept professional judgment visible during the design process. The findings suggest that, in complex professional tasks, GenAI may support reflection and pedagogical reasoning alongside design work.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents translate software interfaces at scale, yet production evidence on what breaks—and which safeguards catch it—is nearly absent: a 2026 mapping study of localization testing retained 24 primary studies, though none on LLM-driven localization. We report a multi-case study of fourteen shipped mobile apps by one developer (ten iOS, four Android; 40–76 locales; roughly 347,000 units) at five maturity levels. Mining the repositories (catalogs, 4473 commits, process documents, tooling), we code defects into thirteen classes in two waves, the second under a frozen codebook, and map each to its detecting layer. Translation quality is not independently measured; the defect record is a lower bound. Of 468 commit-anchored defects, process and coverage gaps—strings escaping the pipeline—are modal in each wave (26.7% and 27.5%); placeholder errors are near-absent (9 in 347,000 units). LLM judges are the largest operational detector (26.7%), ahead of humans (16.0%) and validators (13.7%), yet 127 defects (27.1%) escaped every layer until our audit. What escapes tracks validator scope, not maturity alone. Layered validation, not prompt-level care, determines what reaches users. Translation takes minutes; the validation stack is the lasting cost. We derive six testable propositions and ten guidelines, and release the codebook, dataset, and scripts.

AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

Sitanala is committed to strengthening patient safety culture toward a smart hospital paradigm through an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven innovation named Si Aman EduBot. This interactive chatbot, integrated via WhatsApp and the hospital's proprietary application, was developed to provide real-time education on safety standards, emergency procedures, and digital incident reporting systems for both staff and patients. This study aims to evaluate the impact of Si Aman EduBot implementation on enhancing safety culture within the hospital environment. The evaluation results over a three-month period demonstrated significant achievements, including over 5,000 user interactions, a 35% increase in incident reporting volume, and a 20% improvement in patient safety culture scores from the baseline. The rapid and responsive nature of the chatbot proved effective in increasing staff awareness and fostering an open, blame-free reporting culture. Through its interactive educational features and digital system integration, Si Aman EduBot holds the potential to serve as a national model for building a sustainable patient safety culture. Future developments will focus on integrating voice assistant capabilities and electronic medical records. Keywords: Patient Safety, Educational Chatbot, Digital Incident Reporting, Blame-Free Culture.
